observation.visible_scene: A close-up of a testing/crushing setup against a flat olive-green background. A large metallic tool occupies the upper center: a smooth cylindrical shank that tapers into a worn, conical tip pointing downward. Below it sits a polished cylindrical metal base/anvil with a small notch on its left rim. Trapped between the cone tip and the top face of the base is a pile of fragmented material: dark angular chunks mixed with a lighter tan/yellowish powder, plus scattered fine grains. The base and the upper tool are framed at a fixed position; the background and the base do not shift between frames, indicating a stationary camera.
visible_changes: The conical tool tip remains in continuous contact with the debris pile throughout the segment; it does not visibly lift off or fully crush the pile to the base within these frames.

The debris pile shows only very slight rearrangement/settling: a few dark fragments and tan pieces shift marginally in height and spread, and the pile appears to flatten/spread a touch toward the right in later frames compared with early ones.

Small bright specks (likely dust particles or fine ejected grains) appear and disappear in the air/background around the pile, e.g. on the left side in several mid/late frames, suggesting minor particle motion rather than a large ejection event.
The base cylinder, the upper tool body, and the background stay fixed in position, so any apparent change is object-level (debris/particles), not camera motion.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the tool was actively descending before this segment or continues to descend after it (the clip shows a sustained/slow state, not a clear start or completion of contact).
The identity of the fragmented material and the exact nature of the test (crush, compaction, etc.).
Any outcome beyond the last frame (e.g., full collapse of the pile or tool retracting).
uncertain_details: The vertical position of the conical tip relative to the base changes so little between the first and last frame that a true downward motion of the tool cannot be confirmed; it may be essentially static under load.
The small bright specks in the field of view could be airborne particles, settling grains, or sensor/compression noise; their motion is not clearly trackable.
The degree of debris compression is marginal and could partly reflect lighting/reflection changes on the wet-looking metal rather than physical settling.
